1.title: The Git Mental Model
1.text: Welcome to Module one: The Git Mental Model. It covers the exam area Part one: Foundations. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do seven things. Explain the working tree, staging area and repository. Describe a commit as a snapshot with message, author and parents. Name the four object types and inspect them with git cat-file. Read hashes and short hashes. Explain a branch as a movable pointer and head as the current branch. Find the pointer files inside.git. Practice with exam-style questions and a recall check.

1.title: Three areas: working tree, staging area, repository
1.text: Three areas: working tree, staging area, repository. Every Git command moves content between three areas. The figure shows them, and the table names what each one holds.

1.title: Three areas: working tree, staging area, repository, continued
1.text: Three areas: working tree, staging area, repository. The figure shows this: Three areas: the working tree holds the files you edit, the staging area holds the next snapshot, and the repository holds the committed history.

1.title: Three areas: working tree, staging area, repository, continued
1.text: Three areas: working tree, staging area, repository. Working tree. What it holds: The files you see and edit. Where it lives: Your project folder. What moves content in: Your editor. Staging area (index). What it holds: The proposed next snapshot. Where it lives: dot git slash index. What moves content in: git add. Repository. What it holds: Every commit ever made. Where it lives: dot git slash objects. What moves content in: git commit. git add copies the current content of a file into the staging area. git commit turns the staging area into a new commit. Because staging is a separate step, you choose which changes go into a commit.

1.title: Three areas: working tree, staging area, repository, continued
1.text: Three areas: working tree, staging area, repository. So one file can exist in three versions at once. git show head cart dot txt reads the repository, git show cart dot txt reads the staging area (the colon means the index), and cat reads the working tree. The short status M M means a staged change plus a newer unstaged one. The example is on the screen; read it line by line when you study.

1.title: Three areas: working tree, staging area, repository, continued
1.text: Three areas: working tree, staging area, repository. The example is on the screen; read it line by line when you study. Tip: A commit contains what is staged, not what is in your folder. If you edit a file after git add, add it again, or the newer edit stays out of the commit.

1.title: What a commit is: snapshots and objects
1.text: What a commit is: snapshots and objects. A commit is a snapshot of the whole project at one moment, plus a message, an author, a committer with a time, and its parent commit. Git does not store diffs; it computes them by comparing two snapshots. A file that did not change is not copied again: the new snapshot points at the same stored content. The first commit has no parent. A merge commit has two (module four). Following the parents from any commit gives the history. Git stores everything as objects of four types.

1.title: What a commit is: snapshots and objects, continued
1.text: What a commit is: snapshots and objects. blob. The content of one file, without its name. tree. One folder: names, modes, and the blobs or trees inside. commit. A tree, the parents, author, committer and message. tag. An annotated tag: a name, a message and the object it marks. git cat file dash t prints the type of an object and git cat file dash p prints its content. Your hashes will differ from the ones below.

1.title: What a commit is: snapshots and objects, continued
1.text: What a commit is: snapshots and objects. The commit holds one tree. The tree lists each file as a blob with mode one hundred thousand six hundred forty-four, and each subfolder as another tree with mode forty thousand. git ls files the stage flag shows the same list for the staging area: mode, blob hash, a stage number of zero, and the path. The example is on the screen; read it line by line when you study.

1.title: What a commit is: snapshots and objects, continued
1.text: What a commit is: snapshots and objects. The example is on the screen; read it line by line when you study. Tip: Use git cat file dash p to look at any object. Nothing in Git is hidden once you know a hash, and reading never changes anything.

1.title: What a commit is: snapshots and objects, continued
1.text: What a commit is: snapshots and objects. An annotated tag is a fourth object type with its own message. A lightweight tag is only a name that points at a commit, so its type is commit (module three).

1.title: Hashes: names made from content
1.text: Hashes: names made from content. Every object has a hash: forty hexadecimal characters computed from its content. The same content always gives the same hash. Two files with identical content share one blob, and an unchanged file keeps its blob in the next snapshot. git hash object readme dot md computes the blob hash of a file. A commit hash covers the tree, the parents, the author and the message. Change any of them, as git commit the amend flag does, and you get a new hash.

1.title: Hashes: names made from content, continued
1.text: Hashes: names made from content. A short hash is the first seven characters by default. Git accepts any prefix that is unambiguous, and git log the oneline flag prints short hashes. Loose objects are stored in dot git slash objects, in a folder named after the first two characters. head. The commit you are on. head tilde one or head caret. Its parent. main. The commit at the tip of that branch. v one dot zero. The commit a tag marks. a one b two c three d. A commit, by short hash. git rev parse turns any of these names into a full hash, and the short flag gives the short form.

1.title: Branches, HEAD and the history graph
1.text: Branches, head and the history graph. A branch is a movable pointer to a commit. It is a small file in dot git slash refs slash heads that holds one hash. When you commit, Git moves the pointer of the current branch to the new commit. Creating a branch only writes another small file, so it is instant and costs almost nothing. head says which branch you are on. The file dot git slash head holds ref refs slash heads slash main. Switching branches rewrites that file and the files in your folder. Branches do not contain commits; they point at them, and each commit points at its parent.

2.title: Branches, HEAD and the history graph, continued
2.text: Branches, head and the history graph. A new branch points at the same commit as the branch you made it from. After one commit on feature, main has not moved, and the new commit's parent is the old tip. head can also hold a raw hash instead of a branch name. That is a detached head (module three). After housekeeping, Git may move a branch into dot git slash packed refs, but git rev parse still finds it. Tip: Look inside dot git to understand, but never edit it by hand. Ask Git with git rev parse and git symbolic ref head instead. Tip: Think of a branch as a sticky note on a commit. Moving the note does not delete commits, and commits with no note on them can be lost.

2.title: Practice Question 1
2.text: Question one. Ada runs git add cart dot txt, then edits cart.txt again and runs git commit dash m Update cart without a second add. What does the new commit contain? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: The staged version, because a commit records the staging area. A commit is built from the staging area, so the later edit stays unstaged until it is added.

2.title: Practice Question 2
2.text: Question two. git status dash s prints M M cart dot txt. What does this tell Bob about the file? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: It has a staged change and a newer change that is not staged. The first M is the staging area against the last commit, and the second M is the working tree against the staging area.

2.title: Practice Question 3
2.text: Question three. cat dot git slash head prints ref refs slash heads slash feature. Cy now makes a commit. Which pointer moves? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: The feature branch moves to the new commit. head names the current branch, and a commit moves that branch forward.

2.title: Practice Question 4
2.text: Question four. Bob runs git cat file dash t head readme dot md. What does it print, and why? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: blob, because it is the content of a single file only. A blob stores the content of one file without its name, and the name lives in the tree.

2.title: Practice Question 5
2.text: Question five. Ada copies readme.md to R E A D M E two.md and stages both files. How many blobs does Git need for the two files? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: One, because the hash comes from the content alone. Identical content gives an identical hash, so both paths point to the same blob.

2.title: Practice Question 6
2.text: Question six. Cy runs git branch feature while on main and nothing else. What did Git create? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: A small file that holds the hash of the current commit. A branch is a pointer, so creating one writes a file with a hash and copies nothing.

2.title: Recall Check 1
2.text: Recall check one. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question one. Name the three areas of Git. Answer: The working tree, the staging area (index) and the repository. Question two. Which four object types does Git store? Answer: Blob, tree, commit and tag. Question three. What does dot git slash head hold while you are on main? Answer: ref refs slash heads slash main.

2.title: Recall Check 2
2.text: Recall check two. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question four. Which command turns a name such as head or main into a full hash? Answer: git rev parse. Question five. How many characters does a default short hash have? Answer: Seven. Question six. How many parents does the first commit of a repository have? Answer: None.

2.title: Module Recap
2.text: Here is the recap. Three areas: Working tree, staging area ( dot git slash index ), repository ( dot git slash objects ). Staging: git add fills the index; a commit records the index, not the folder. Commit: Snapshot plus message, author, committer and parent. Objects: blob (file content), tree (folder), commit, tag; git cat file dash t and dash p. Index listing: git ls files the stage flag shows mode, blob hash, stage zero, path. Hashes: forty hex characters from the content; short hash is seven; git rev parse. Branch: A file in dot git slash refs slash heads holding one commit hash. head: dot git slash head holds ref refs slash heads slash main; commits move the current branch.
